task_reviews.rationale: All twelve negative-copula positions match the actual selected present/preterite indicative system. The explanation preserves separate ne where taught and the contractions nis/næs/nǣre/nǣron; repeated plural spellings retain distinct person positions. Cook78–79 and100 corroborate the negative system. No subjunctive or universal contracted present is inferred.

All twelve nabban forms match the selected negative-possession paradigm, including næfst/næfð, nabbað and the weak preterite series. Four requested meanings distinguish present from past and first singular from third plural. Cook74 with the negative contraction discussion on23 supports the pattern.

All twelve selected negative willan forms match; nelle/nelt/nele/nellað and nolde/noldest/noldon are not confused with negative possession. Four translations preserve volition and tense. The selected e-series is legitimate alongside documented variants, but a selected-series task need not accept every variant as compliance. Cook79 supplies the system.

All six outputs distinguish the actual negative expressions from the single proposition denied in each clause. Negative concord is interpreted as one denial, including the subject/object quantifiers in the third clause; the key supplies complete meanings. Cook100 §183 confirms the construction.

Three outputs correctly distinguish constituent nā from finite ne. The first assertion remains affirmative with self and a contrasted excluded person; the second negates going. The same distinction is required by source31.2.

Ic næfde ðā bōc, and ic nolde gān meets the explicit contracted-preterite targets for possession and volition. The book and refusal to go are both retained; an uncontracted alternative would be grammatical but would miss this stated control.

Hē self gǣð, and nā ōðer keeps the man’s going affirmative and excludes another person through constituent nā. Self agrees with the masculine subject; finite ne would change the requested proposition.

All twenty-four four-case strong nān positions agree with the visible selected table. Masculine accusative nānne, feminine -re obliques, selected feminine plural nāna and neuter endingless forms are all retained. Cook52 states strong nān and Cook39–40 supplies the adjective endings. The explanation distinguishes agreement from syncretism.

All eight personal/neuter singular gehwā positions match the selected hwā-derived forms. Personal gehwone is distinguished from neuter gehwæt. Cook52–53 and Wright240 support the compound and singular distribution. Neither the task nor the key invents plural cells or distinct personal masculine/feminine declensions.

The nine outputs correctly identify interrogative, contingent indefinite and free-choice hwā, give their meanings, and separate subordinate subjects from the main subject/recipient. The actual examples and visible construction teaching supply the distinction; an English analysis is not a new productive paradigm.

All four outputs correctly contrast distributive singular ǣlc with collective plural ealle and identify the actual subject heads/finite agreement. The witness does not infer plural agreement merely from the number of people distributed over.

Five answers preserve the contrast between defective impersonal man and ordinary count mann. Both given finite verbs are singular, but that shared agreement does not erase the reference contrast. Cook53 §89e confirms impersonal nominative singular man.
Four answers preserve anything in an open question, nothing under negation, and something in an affirmative clause. The middle ne/nāwiht combination is one denial, not a positive assertion.
Three answers distinguish the indefinite introduction from the cardinal contrast without inventing different morphology. Both ān forms agree with nominative masculine singular mann.

Nān mann ne hæfð bōc; gehwā hæfð męte preserves both propositions, negative concord and singular distributive gehwā. Both clauses use taught possession syntax; no hidden alternative lexical target is imposed.

The witness’s question uses ǣnige with feminine accusative bōc; its answer uses nāne and finite ne. Both are correct, and the reply’s object-before-verb order differs harmlessly from the model while preserving the actual lexical targets.

Gif hwā bōc hæbbe, ic him pęning sęlle uses indefinite hwā, the requested potential present subjunctive, the possessed book, a resumptive dative recipient and a penny given. Indicative conditions may be valid in other contexts, but this target is explicit and met.
Man mæg gān uses the requested impersonal subject, singular ordinary-ability magan and plain infinitive. It preserves one can go without adding a plural impersonal paradigm.

Ǣlc sunu hæfð āne bōc; ealle ðā suna habbað męte correctly contrasts distributive singular and quantified plural. Āne agrees with feminine accusative bōc; both finite verbs agree with their actual subjects.

Ic nāwiht nānum ne sęlle retains all three explicit negative targets, the accusative thing given and dative recipient, expressing one denial. Substantival nānum is licensed by the unit’s nān as no one; the key’s added męnn is not a hidden requirement.
Nānes mannes sunu ne cymð correctly places the negative dependent genitive within the subject noun phrase and finite ne in the clause. The son is singular subject, not an object of denial.

Se cyning næfð nāna bēc uses the requested contracted possession form and selected feminine accusative plural nāna with bēc. The root-noun plural is correct; a valid uncontracted ne hæfð would not satisfy this particular stated target.

Se cyning gesiehð gehwone; gehwæs sunu is gōd uses personal accusative gehwone as the first direct object and genitive gehwæs as the second clause’s dependent possessor. Both explicit targets and complete propositions are retained.

Ān mann cōm, and hē hæfde bōc correctly introduces an unnamed man and continues with past possession. Bare bōc is valid for an indefinite book; the prompt does not require an exact numerical contrast or an additional ān.
Four answers identify inclusive both-and, each accusative object, and the absence of an exclusive either-or choice. The finite predicate and the son’s possession are preserved.

Three answers correctly analyze the ordinary resumed free-choice pattern. Hwā’s nominative is set by its own clause and him’s dative by main-clause giving; source31.12’s separately supplied attraction is not imposed here.

Four answers distinguish personal genitive dual uncer in ānum uncer from the agreeing possessive uncer in uncer hūs. The external recipient remains dative and only one of the two is selected. Earlier pronoun teaching and Cook90 partitive genitive support the analysis.

Swā hwā swā gā, ic him pęning sęlle meets the free-choice frame and present subjunctive target, with dative resumption and the complete promise. The analysis does not replace whoever with a merely factual condition.

Swā hwæðer ðissa twēgra suna swā ǣrest cume, ic him ðā bōc sęlle correctly preserves the two-son group, internal nominative subject, first arrival, present subjunctive and explicit main dative. It does not import the separately supplied source-specific attraction of31.12.
Ic gesēo ǣgðer ge ðone cyning ge his sunu includes both accusative objects in the requested inclusive construction. The possession relation his sunu and the seeing predicate are retained.

All six outputs distinguish equal degree, preference and proportional correlation. The standards retain their original syntactic roles; the feminine pronoun in the third sentence refers to bōc. The analyses match the actual inputs rather than importing one universal swā meaning.
Swā ðæt hūs māre is, swā hit bętere is gives the requested proportional comparison. Both comparatives fit the neuter singular house and hit resumes it; this is not the equality construction.
Ðēos bōc is swā gōd swā sēo bōc, ac ðæs cyninges bōc is bętere preserves this/that, equal goodness and the king’s better book. The feminine nominative comparative and dependent genitive are correct.
Hē lufað męte swīðor ðonne wīn preserves preference and the requested swīðor construction. Męte and wīn are parallel accusative objects, so the standard is not falsely recast as a subject.

Both complete eight-position root-noun paradigms match: bōc/bēc/bōca/bōcum and tōð/tōðes/tēð/tōða/tōðum. The explanations identify the different umlaut distributions and each syncretic surface. Cook31–32 and36 support the root patterns and recorded alternatives, without promoting alternatives to the selected-cell target.

Wright184 corroborates the feminine abstract class and its variants; the BT500b hǣlu entry explicitly supports indeclinability. The key and witness correctly leave plural meanings unassigned rather than claiming historical nonexistence.
